claims.text: A two-step transfer-learning workflow can faithfully reproduce solid free energies near melting.
The workflow can faithfully reproduce liquid free energies near melting.
The workflow can retain vibrational-entropy contributions.
The workflow can retain anharmonic contributions.
The workflow can retain electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The workflow will substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
An initial machine-learned potential will be trained using a large dataset generated by inexpensive molecular dynamics or empirical-potential molecular dynamics.
Targeted ab initio free-energy evaluations of both solid and liquid phases near melting will be used to refine the machine-learned potential.
Periodic correction by ab initio free-energy benchmarks enables the machine-learned potential-energy surface to capture anharmonic contributions in both phases.
Periodic correction by ab initio free-energy benchmarks enables the machine-learned potential-energy surface to capture electron–vibration contributions in both phases.
Using an iteratively refined surrogate potential reduces the number of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics evaluations required.
Transfer learning improves sampling efficiency while periodic ab initio anchoring preserves free-energy accuracy.
The proposed method will be approximately an order of magnitude faster than full ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows.
The proposed method will be faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The proposed method will maintain free-energy errors within approximately 5–10 meV per atom.
The proposed method will maintain melting-temperature errors within tens of kelvin.
The initial validation domain is elemental and binary metallic systems near their melting points.
The proposed applicability domain may extend to alloys containing up to four or five components when similar free-energy landscapes are encountered.
